<meta>continues from previous page: but he included</meta> all provinces and regions in a single type of calamity. Thus, we have seen Massilia <note>modern Marseille, a long-standing ally of Rome that was besieged and stripped of its independence by Julius Caesar</note> harassed and, after its foreign possessions were lost, carried in a triumph as an example to other nations; we saw a triumph celebrated over that city without which our commanders never celebrated a triumph from Transalpine wars. I could mention many other wicked acts against our allies, if the sun had ever seen anything more unworthy than this one case alone. We are therefore justly punished. For unless we had allowed the crimes of many to go unpunished, such unbridled license would never have reached a single man <note>referring to the rise of an absolute dictator</note>. From him, indeed, the inheritance of private property came to the greed of a few, and to many wicked men.

Nor will the seed of civil wars ever be absent from our cause as long as desperate men remember and hope for that <term>hasta</term> <gloss>spear</gloss> <note>a spear was traditionally stuck into the ground to signify a public auction, here specifically the auction of property confiscated from proscribed citizens</note> dripping with blood. For when Sulla had brandished it while his kinsman was dictator, thirty-six years later he did not withdraw from an even more wicked spear. Another, however, who had been a clerk in that earlier dictatorship, was the urban <term>quaestor</term> <gloss>a public treasurer or magistrate</gloss> in this one. From this, it should be understood that as long as such rewards are offered, civil wars will never be lacking. And so, only the walls of the city stand and remain, and even these now fear the most extreme crimes; but we have utterly lost the Republic itself. And we have fallen into these disasters. For we must return to our premise: while we were feared, we preferred to be loved as long as we were dear. If these things could happen to the Roman people even while they ruled justly, what ought individuals to think?

<insert>On gaining affection</insert>

But since it is clear that the power of goodwill is great and that of fear is weak, it follows that we should discuss by what means we can most easily attain that which we desire: affection joined with honor and trust. But these things are not equally...

<summary>Cicero argues that the decline of Roman morality and the rise of dictatorships resulted from a shift from being loved to being feared. He cites the mistreatment of allies like Massilia and the recurring horror of the auction spear as evidence of the Republic's collapse.</summary>
<keywords>Massilia, Sulla, civil war, dictator, quaestor, public auction, Republic, justice, fear versus love</keywords>
